specStatements.text: All bodies (objects), no matter what temperature, emit and absorb infrared radiation. The hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time.

A perfect black body is an object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it. A black body does not reflect or transmit any radiation. Since a good absorber is also a good emitter, a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter.
Students should be able to explain:
• that the intensity and wavelength distribution of any emission depends on the temperature of the body.

(HT only) A body at constant temperature is absorbing radiation at the same rate as it is emitting radiation. The temperature of a body increases when the body absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation.
(HT only) The temperature of the Earth depends on many factors including: the rates of absorption and emission of radiation, reflection of radiation into space.

(HT only) Students should be able to explain how the temperature of a body is related to the balance between incoming radiation absorbed and radiation emitted, using everyday examples to illustrate this balance, and the example of the factors which determine the temperature of the Earth.
(HT only) Students should be able to use information, or draw/interpret diagrams to show how radiation affects the temperature of the Earth’s surface and atmosphere.

scopeNotes.statement: • that the intensity and wavelength distribution of any emission depends on the temperature of the body.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification asks only that students explain that intensity and wavelength distribution DEPEND on temperature. The content therefore stays qualitative: as a body gets hotter it emits more radiation at every wavelength and the peak of the distribution moves to shorter wavelengths. No radiation law is named or used - there is no Wien displacement calculation, no Stefan-Boltzmann fourth-power relationship, no photon energy and no absolute-temperature algebra. Graph questions ask students to compare two curves qualitatively, which is what the word 'distribution' requires, and nothing is assessed that would need a formula the specification does not give.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) A body at constant temperature is absorbing radiation at the same rate as it is emitting radiation. The temperature of a body increases when the body absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every item built from this statement and from the three that follow it is marked 'higher', because the specification flags all of 4.6.3.2's balance content as HT only. Foundation-tier students meet emission and absorption by all bodies, the black body definition and the temperature dependence of emission (S01, S02, S04, S05) but are never asked here about rates of absorption and emission balancing, about the factors setting the Earth's temperature, or about interpreting Earth radiation diagrams. The reasoning is also kept to rates, as the specification words it, and is never turned into an energy-transfer calculation or a specific heat capacity problem.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) The temperature of the Earth depends on many factors including: the rates of absorption and emission of radiation, reflection of radiation into space.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification names three factors and says 'many factors including', so the named three are treated as the assessable core and nothing beyond them is required. Greenhouse gases are used only as the mechanism by which the atmosphere absorbs and re-emits infrared radiation - that is the 'rates of absorption and emission' factor applied to the atmosphere - and no student is asked to name individual gases, quantify their contributions, discuss climate policy, ocean circulation, albedo as a numerical quantity, or the carbon cycle. Diagram questions use only arrows for incoming, reflected, absorbed and emitted radiation, which is the level the statement supports.

concepts.definition: Electromagnetic radiation emitted by every object because of its temperature. All bodies, no matter what temperature they are, both emit and absorb infrared radiation - a block of ice, a person and a hot oven are all emitting it at the same time as they absorb it from their surroundings.

concepts.term: Emission and absorption by all bodies
concepts.definition: Emitting radiation means giving it out; absorbing radiation means taking it in. These happen together and continuously: an object does not have to be hot to emit, and it does not stop absorbing while it emits. What changes from object to object is the rate at which each happens.

concepts.term: Effect of temperature on the rate of emission
concepts.definition: The hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time. Two identical objects at different temperatures both emit, but the hotter one emits more radiation every second.

An object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it. A black body does not reflect or transmit any radiation. It is an idealised object - a model - not simply an object whose surface happens to look black.

Radiation arriving at a surface can bounce off it (reflect), pass through it (transmit) or be taken in by it (absorb). A perfect black body does none of the first two, so all of the incident radiation is absorbed.

concepts.term: A good absorber is a good emitter
concepts.definition: A surface that absorbs radiation well also emits it well. Since a perfect black body absorbs all of the radiation incident on it, it is the best possible absorber, and therefore a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter.

How much radiation a body emits - loosely, the energy radiated per second from each square metre of its surface. Intensity is one of the two things about an emission that depend on the temperature of the body.

A body does not emit at one single wavelength. It emits over a range of wavelengths, with more intensity at some wavelengths than at others, and this spread is called the wavelength distribution. It is usually shown as a graph of intensity against wavelength.

The intensity and wavelength distribution of any emission depends on the temperature of the body. As a body gets hotter, the intensity increases at every wavelength and the peak of the distribution moves to shorter wavelengths - which is why a heated metal bar first feels warm, then glows dull red, then glows orange and finally white.

Any object in a room - a book, a wall, a person - is emitting radiation and absorbing radiation from everything around it at the same time. Explaining an everyday observation starts from that fact rather than from the idea that only hot objects radiate.

A body at constant temperature is absorbing radiation at the same rate as it is emitting radiation. Both processes are still happening; the two rates are simply equal, so the temperature does not change.

The temperature of a body increases when the body absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation. If instead it emits faster than it absorbs, its temperature falls. It is the difference between the two rates that decides the direction of the change.

Some of the radiation arriving at the Earth is reflected straight back into space by clouds, by ice and snow and by other light surfaces. Radiation that is reflected is not absorbed, so it does not raise the temperature of the surface it bounced off.

concepts.term: Factors determining the temperature of the Earth
concepts.definition: The temperature of the Earth depends on many factors including: the rates of absorption and emission of radiation, and reflection of radiation into space. The Earth's temperature settles where the total rate of absorption equals the total rate of emission back into space.

The same balance explains everyday cooling and warming. A hot drink emits faster than it absorbs, so it cools until the two rates match at room temperature; a car parked in sunshine absorbs faster than it emits, so it warms until the rising rate of emission catches up.

A typical diagram shows radiation from the hot Sun arriving mainly at short wavelengths; some is reflected back into space; the rest is absorbed by the surface and the atmosphere. The much cooler Earth then emits at longer infrared wavelengths, and gases in the atmosphere absorb some of this and re-emit it, part of it back towards the surface. Reading the arrows lets you compare the rates of absorption and emission.

misconceptions.question: A block of ice is far too cold to emit any infrared radiation.
misconceptions.correct: All bodies (objects), no matter what temperature, emit and absorb infrared radiation, so the ice emits infrared radiation - just less each second than a warmer object would.
misconceptions.misconception: Only hot things give out infrared radiation; cold things just take it in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Infrared is introduced through hot objects - grills, heaters, thermal images of warm bodies - and 'radiates heat' sounds like something only a heat source can do. Thermal images of cold objects look dark, which students read as 'nothing coming out'.
misconceptions.correction: Emission never switches off. Temperature controls the rate, not whether it happens: the hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time. A thermal camera can still form an image of a block of ice because the ice is emitting.

misconceptions.question: An object only emits radiation if it is hotter than the air around it.
misconceptions.correct: Every object emits radiation all the time, whatever its surroundings are doing. Being cooler than its surroundings changes the balance between emission and absorption, not whether emission occurs.
misconceptions.misconception: Radiation only comes out of something when it is warmer than its surroundings - otherwise it just absorbs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the rule for conduction and convection, where net energy transfer needs a temperature difference, onto emission itself. Net cooling and emission get treated as the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two rates. A cool object in a warm room is emitting and absorbing at the same time; it absorbs faster than it emits, so it warms up. Emission is happening throughout.

misconceptions.question: Anything painted matt black is a perfect black body.
misconceptions.correct: A perfect black body is an object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it and neither reflects nor transmits any. Matt black paint is a good approximation, but no real surface absorbs every bit of incident radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: A black body just means an object that is black in colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The name invites it, and black surfaces really are the best everyday absorbers, so the everyday meaning of 'black' is close enough to feel right.
misconceptions.correction: The definition is about behaviour, not colour: absorbs all incident radiation, reflects none, transmits none. It is an idealised model that real surfaces only approach.

misconceptions.question: A surface that absorbs radiation well must be poor at emitting it, because it holds the energy in.
misconceptions.correct: A good absorber is also a good emitter. That is exactly why a perfect black body, the best possible absorber, would be the best possible emitter.
misconceptions.misconception: Good absorbers keep energy in, so they must be bad emitters.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Absorbing' sounds like storing, and insulation lessons teach that keeping energy in is a property of a surface. Students think of absorption and emission as opposites that cannot both be strong.
misconceptions.correction: Absorption and emission depend on the same surface property. A matt black car left in the sun gets hottest during the day and also cools fastest at night - the same surface is good at both.

misconceptions.question: A perfect black body absorbs all radiation, so it never emits any.
misconceptions.correct: A perfect black body absorbs all of the radiation incident on it AND is the best possible emitter of radiation.
misconceptions.misconception: A black body swallows radiation and traps it, so nothing ever comes back out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Absorbs everything' sounds final, and the phrase 'black hole' sits nearby in students' minds. Nothing in the word 'absorb' suggests the object is radiating at the same time.
misconceptions.correction: The specification pairs the two: since a good absorber is also a good emitter, a perfect black body would be the best possible emitter. If it absorbed without emitting, its temperature would rise without limit, which does not happen.

misconceptions.question: Heating a body changes the wavelengths it emits but not how much it emits.
misconceptions.correct: The intensity and wavelength distribution of any emission depends on the temperature of the body - both change. A hotter body emits more intensely at every wavelength and its peak moves to shorter wavelengths.
misconceptions.misconception: Making something hotter just shifts the colour; the total amount coming out stays the same.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour change is the visible effect, so it takes all the attention. On a graph, students notice the peak sliding sideways and overlook the whole curve rising.
misconceptions.correction: Compare two curves properly: the hotter curve lies above the cooler one at every wavelength as well as peaking further to the left. Both intensity and distribution respond to temperature.

misconceptions.question: Heating a body makes it emit more radiation, but always at the same wavelengths.
misconceptions.correct: Raising the temperature increases the intensity and changes the wavelength distribution; the peak of the distribution moves to shorter wavelengths.
misconceptions.misconception: Temperature controls how much radiation comes out, and that is all it controls.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Hotter means more radiation each second' is the first rule students learn, and it is correct as far as it goes. Nothing in it hints that the mix of wavelengths changes too.
misconceptions.correction: Watch a heating element: it is invisible when warm, dull red when hotter, then orange. The wavelengths emitted have clearly changed, not only the amount.

misconceptions.question: If a body stays at a constant temperature, it has stopped absorbing and emitting radiation.
misconceptions.correct: A body at constant temperature is absorbing radiation at the same rate as it is emitting radiation. Both processes continue; the rates are equal.
misconceptions.misconception: Nothing is happening when the temperature is steady - the radiation has stopped.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Nothing changing' is read as 'nothing happening'. Students have not yet met the idea of a dynamic balance, where two opposite processes run at equal rates.
misconceptions.correction: Constant temperature is a balance, not a stop. The Earth's surface absorbs and emits enormous amounts of radiation every second while its temperature barely changes from day to day.

misconceptions.question: Any body that is absorbing radiation must be getting hotter.
misconceptions.correct: The temperature of a body increases only when the body absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation. A body can absorb steadily and still cool, if it is emitting even faster.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Absorption is taught as energy going in, so it feels as though it must raise the temperature. The simultaneous emission is easy to forget.
misconceptions.misconception: Absorbing radiation always warms something up.
misconceptions.correction: Only the difference between the two rates matters. A hot drink in a warm room is absorbing radiation from the room the whole time it cools, because it is emitting faster than it absorbs.

misconceptions.question: Something warms up when it emits more radiation than it absorbs.
misconceptions.correct: The temperature of a body increases when the body absorbs radiation faster than it emits radiation. Emitting faster than absorbing makes the temperature fall.
misconceptions.misconception: Giving out radiation is what makes things hot, so more emission means a higher temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hot objects do emit strongly, so students reverse cause and effect - the strong emission is the result of the high temperature, not the cause. The words 'radiating heat' make emission sound like heating.
misconceptions.correction: Track the direction of energy transfer. Radiation emitted leaves the body, so emitting faster than absorbing cools it; radiation absorbed arrives, so absorbing faster than emitting warms it.

misconceptions.question: Radiation reflected by clouds and ice still warms the Earth's surface.
misconceptions.correct: Radiation reflected back into space is not absorbed, so it transfers no energy to the surface. Reflection of radiation into space is one of the factors that keeps the Earth's temperature down.
misconceptions.misconception: The radiation is still there bouncing about, so it warms the ground anyway.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture reflected radiation as staying inside the system. Diagrams draw the reflected arrow near the surface, which makes it look as though it lingers there.
misconceptions.correction: Only absorbed radiation transfers energy to a body. A reflected ray leaves for space; a snow-covered field reflects far more than dark soil does and so warms up much less in the same sunshine.

misconceptions.question: The temperature of the Earth is set purely by how much radiation arrives from the Sun.
misconceptions.correct: The temperature of the Earth depends on many factors including: the rates of absorption and emission of radiation, reflection of radiation into space.
misconceptions.misconception: Incoming sunlight is the only thing that decides how warm the Earth is.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Sun is the obvious source, and everyday experience links sunshine directly with warmth. What leaves the Earth is invisible and easy to leave out of the account.
misconceptions.correction: Incoming radiation is only one side. How much is reflected straight back, how much is absorbed and how fast the Earth and its atmosphere emit back into space all matter, and the temperature settles where absorption and emission balance.

misconceptions.question: Gases in the atmosphere trap radiation, and that is the end of it.
misconceptions.correct: Gases in the atmosphere absorb infrared radiation emitted by the Earth's surface and then emit radiation themselves, some of it back towards the surface and some out into space.
misconceptions.misconception: The atmosphere works like a lid - radiation gets stuck under it and cannot get out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'trapped' is used loosely in everyday and even textbook language, and greenhouse diagrams often draw a barrier. Absorbing bodies being emitters too is the step that gets skipped.
misconceptions.correction: The atmosphere absorbs and emits, like any other body. It is a good absorber of infrared and therefore also a good emitter, and it is the radiation it emits back downwards that keeps the surface warmer than it would otherwise be.

misconceptions.question: The Earth's surface sends back the same radiation it received from the Sun.
misconceptions.correct: The Sun is far hotter than the Earth, so it emits mainly short-wavelength radiation, while the much cooler Earth emits at longer infrared wavelengths.
misconceptions.misconception: Radiation absorbed by the ground is simply re-radiated exactly as it came in.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Arrows in and arrows out look alike on a diagram, and students who have not linked the emitted wavelengths to temperature have no reason to expect them to differ.
misconceptions.correction: Use the rule that the wavelength distribution depends on temperature. The Sun at thousands of degrees emits mainly visible and near-infrared; the Earth's surface, near 15 °C, emits longer-wavelength infrared - which is why atmospheric gases can absorb the outgoing radiation but not most of the incoming.

options.text: Only objects hot enough to glow red, orange or white
options.rationale: A student who ties radiation to visible heat sources picks the glowing objects.

options.text: All objects, whatever their temperature happens to be
options.rationale: All bodies (objects), no matter what temperature, emit and absorb infrared radiation.

options.text: Only objects that are warmer than the air around them
options.rationale: Transfers the temperature-difference rule for conduction onto emission itself.

options.text: Only objects with a dull, dark or matt black surface
options.rationale: Confuses being a good emitter with being the only emitter.

mcqs.stem: Two identical metal blocks sit in the same room. Block X is at 80 °C and block Y is at 20 °C. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Only X radiates infrared, because Y is not hot at all
options.rationale: Treats emission as something only hot objects do rather than a rate that varies.

options.text: X radiates more infrared each second than Y does
options.rationale: The hotter the body, the more infrared radiation it radiates in a given time.

options.text: Y radiates nothing but absorbs the infrared from X
options.rationale: The cooler block is seen as a receiver only, because it is gaining energy overall.

options.text: Both blocks radiate infrared at exactly the same rate
options.rationale: 'Identical blocks' is read as identical behaviour, ignoring the temperature difference.

mcqs.stem: What is a perfect black body?

options.text: An object whose surface is matt black rather than shiny
options.rationale: Reads the name as a description of colour instead of behaviour.

options.text: An object that absorbs radiation and never emits any of it
options.rationale: 'Absorbs everything' is taken to mean nothing comes back out.

options.text: An object that absorbs all of the radiation incident on it
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition; it reflects and transmits none of it.

options.text: An object that reflects no radiation but transmits it all
options.rationale: Picks up 'does not reflect' but forgets that it does not transmit either.

mcqs.stem: Why would a perfect black body be the best possible emitter of radiation?

options.text: It stores all the radiation it takes in and keeps it inside
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think absorbing well means holding energy in.

options.text: Its black surface reflects radiation better than a shiny one
options.rationale: Muddles reflection with emission, and a black body reflects nothing.

options.text: It transmits radiation straight through itself very quickly
options.rationale: Confuses transmitting radiation through an object with emitting new radiation.

options.text: A good absorber of radiation is also a good emitter of it
options.rationale: Absorption and emission depend on the same surface property, so the best absorber is the best emitter.

mcqs.stem: A book has been lying on a shelf in a cool room for several hours. Which statement about the book is correct?

options.text: It is emitting infrared radiation and absorbing it as well
options.rationale: All bodies emit radiation, and the book absorbs radiation from its surroundings at the same time.

options.text: It is absorbing infrared radiation but is too cool to emit
options.rationale: Emission is treated as something reserved for hot objects.

options.text: It emits radiation only when it is warmer than the room
options.rationale: Applies a temperature-difference condition to emission rather than to the net change.

options.text: It emits visible light that is far too dim for us to see
options.rationale: Assumes all bodies emit visible light, when at room temperature the emission is infrared.

mcqs.stem: What does the emission from a body depend on?

options.text: Its temperature, which sets the intensity but not the wavelengths
options.rationale: Keeps the familiar 'hotter means more' rule and omits the change in distribution.

options.text: Its temperature, which sets the wavelengths but not the intensity
options.rationale: Notices only the colour change that heating produces.

options.text: Its temperature, which sets both the intensity and the wavelengths
options.rationale: The intensity and wavelength distribution of any emission depends on the temperature of the body.

options.text: Its colour, which sets both the intensity and the wavelengths
options.rationale: Substitutes the surface colour for temperature as the controlling variable.

mcqs.stem: A graph shows how the intensity of the radiation emitted by a body varies with wavelength, at 3000 K and again at 4000 K. Compared with the 3000 K curve, the 4000 K curve is:

options.text: the same height overall, with its peak at a shorter wavelength
options.rationale: Sees the peak slide sideways but not the whole curve rise.

options.text: higher at every wavelength, with its peak at a shorter wavelength
options.rationale: Raising the temperature lifts the whole curve and moves the peak towards shorter wavelengths.

options.text: higher at every wavelength, with its peak at the same wavelength
options.rationale: Applies 'hotter emits more' without letting the distribution change.

options.text: lower at every wavelength, with its peak at a longer wavelength
options.rationale: Reverses both effects, as if the hotter body radiated less.

mcqs.stem: A central heating radiator is switched off and cools until it is at room temperature. Which statement is then correct?

options.text: It has stopped emitting radiation because it is not hot now
options.rationale: Ties emission to being hot rather than to temperature setting a rate.

options.text: It still emits radiation, but less each second than before
options.rationale: Emission never stops; the lower temperature simply means a lower rate of emission.

options.text: It now only absorbs the radiation coming from the warm air
options.rationale: Assumes an object at the same temperature as its surroundings can only absorb.

options.text: It emits radiation only while its temperature is changing
options.rationale: Links emission to a change of temperature rather than to temperature itself.

mcqs.stem: A body stays at a constant temperature. What must be true?

options.text: It absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits radiation
options.rationale: Constant temperature is a balance between the two rates, which both continue.

options.text: It has completely stopped absorbing and emitting radiation
options.rationale: 'Nothing changing' is read as 'nothing happening'.

options.text: It emits radiation at a faster rate than it absorbs it
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think emission is what sustains a temperature.

options.text: It absorbs no radiation, so its temperature cannot rise
options.rationale: Assumes any absorption at all would have to make the temperature climb.

mcqs.stem: The temperature of a body is rising. Which statement describes what is happening?

options.text: It is emitting radiation faster than it is absorbing radiation
options.rationale: Reverses cause and effect: strong emission is a result of high temperature, not its cause.

options.text: It is absorbing radiation and is not emitting any radiation
options.rationale: Treats warming as proof that emission has been switched off.

options.text: It is absorbing radiation faster than it is emitting radiation
options.rationale: The temperature of a body increases when it absorbs radiation faster than it emits it.

options.text: It is absorbing and emitting radiation at exactly equal rates
options.rationale: Confuses the condition for constant temperature with the condition for warming.

mcqs.stem: Snow-covered ground reflects far more of the Sun's radiation than bare dark soil does. What is the effect of this?

options.text: The reflected radiation warms the ground as it leaves
options.rationale: Pictures reflected radiation as lingering at the surface and heating it.

options.text: The ground absorbs the reflected radiation a moment later
options.rationale: Keeps the reflected radiation inside the system rather than losing it to space.

options.text: The ground emits faster to make up for the reflection
options.rationale: Invents a compensating emission, treating emission as a response that restores warmth.

options.text: Less radiation is absorbed, so the ground stays colder
options.rationale: Only absorbed radiation transfers energy to the ground; reflection into space removes it.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the factors that determine the temperature of the Earth is correct?

options.text: It depends on the rates of absorption and emission, and on reflection
options.rationale: The specification names the rates of absorption and emission of radiation and reflection of radiation into space.

options.text: It depends only on how much radiation reaches the Earth from the Sun
options.rationale: Counts the incoming radiation and ignores what is reflected and emitted.

options.text: It depends only on how much radiation the atmosphere can trap in
options.rationale: Reduces everything to a single 'trapping' mechanism.

options.text: It depends only on how far the Earth is from the Sun at the time
options.rationale: Picks one plausible astronomical factor and treats it as the whole answer.

mcqs.stem: A cup of tea is left in a room and slowly cools down. Using ideas about radiation, which statement is correct?

options.text: It absorbs radiation faster than it emits it, and so it cools
options.rationale: Reverses which rate must be larger for the temperature to fall.

options.text: It stops absorbing any radiation as soon as it begins to cool
options.rationale: Assumes a cooling object can only be emitting, not absorbing.

options.text: It absorbs radiation, so its temperature must be increasing
options.rationale: Treats any absorption as proof of warming, ignoring the larger emission.

options.text: It emits radiation faster than it absorbs it, so it cools
options.rationale: Emitting faster than absorbing lowers the temperature; both processes continue throughout.

mcqs.stem: A greenhouse warms up through the morning and then stays at a steady temperature all afternoon. Which statement about the afternoon is correct?

options.text: It absorbs and emits radiation at equal rates, so it stays steady
options.rationale: A body at constant temperature absorbs radiation at the same rate as it emits radiation.

options.text: It has stopped absorbing and emitting radiation, so it stays steady
options.rationale: Reads an unchanging temperature as the processes having ceased.

options.text: It cannot absorb any more radiation once it has stopped warming
options.rationale: Assumes that absorbing must always mean the temperature is still rising.

options.text: It absorbed radiation all morning and only emits it in the afternoon
options.rationale: Treats the greenhouse as storing radiation and releasing it later, in sequence.

mcqs.stem: A diagram shows radiation arriving at the Earth from the Sun and radiation leaving the Earth's surface. Which statement comparing them is correct?

options.text: The Earth sends back the same wavelengths that arrived at it
options.rationale: Reads the outgoing arrow as the incoming radiation simply bouncing back.

options.text: The Earth emits shorter wavelengths because its surface is solid
options.rationale: Uses the state of the surface instead of its temperature to set the wavelengths.

options.text: The Earth emits nothing, as the atmosphere holds the radiation in
options.rationale: Treats the atmosphere as a lid that stops any emission escaping the surface.

options.text: The Earth is much cooler, so it emits at longer wavelengths
options.rationale: The wavelength distribution depends on temperature, and the Earth is far cooler than the Sun.

mcqs.stem: On a diagram of the Earth's energy balance, the surface is shown absorbing radiation at 168 W/m² and emitting radiation at 168 W/m². What does this tell you?

options.text: The surface has stopped absorbing and emitting radiation now
options.rationale: Equal arrows are misread as no radiation being exchanged at all.

options.text: The surface is warming, because it is absorbing radiation
options.rationale: Sees the absorption figure alone and concludes the temperature must rise.

options.text: The surface temperature stays constant while both continue
options.rationale: Equal rates of absorption and emission mean the temperature does not change.

options.text: The surface is cooling, because radiation escapes to space
options.rationale: Sees the emission figure alone and concludes the surface must be losing out.
